name: ghidra
plain: Ghidra takes a compiled program (which you cannot read) and turns it back into something you can: assembly instructions, and a rough reconstruction of the original C code called the decompilation. You then read what the program does without having its source.
In CTFs it is the main tool for 'reverse engineering' challenges: find the check that compares your input with the flag, or find the vulnerable function in a pwn binary.
You work inside a project: create a project, import the binary, double-click it to open the CodeBrowser, say yes to analysis, and then explore. Ghidra starts with `ghidraRun`.
when: Find the function that validates a password or a flag.
Read strings and see where each is used.
Understand a binary's control flow before exploiting it.
Rename functions and variables as you learn what they do.
Compare what the decompiler says with the assembly.

examples.title: Open a binary
examples.cmd: ghidraRun  >  File > New Project (Non-Shared) > File > Import File > double-click the file > Yes to analyze > OK
examples.explain: Import detects the format (ELF, PE) and architecture. The default analysis options are fine for a first pass. Wait for the progress bar at the bottom right.

examples.title: Find main
examples.cmd: Symbol Tree (left) > Functions > main   or   Navigation > Go To... (G) > type main
examples.explain: On stripped binaries main is not named: look for entry, then the function it passes to __libc_start_main.

examples.title: Read the decompiler
examples.cmd: Select a function. The right pane (Decompile) shows C-like code. Click a variable to highlight all uses.
examples.explain: It is a good guess, not the truth. Variable names are invented (local_28, param_1) and types may be wrong.

examples.title: Rename something
examples.cmd: Click a name, press L, type a new name, Enter
examples.explain: Renaming local_28 to input_buf makes the rest of the function read like English. Do it as you learn.

examples.title: Fix a variable's type
examples.cmd: Click a variable in the decompiler, press Ctrl+L, enter e.g. char[32]
examples.explain: A correct type often untangles an array access that looked like a mess.

examples.title: Search for interesting strings
examples.cmd: Window > Defined Strings   (or Search > For Strings...)
examples.explain: Look for 'flag', 'correct', 'wrong', 'password'. Double-click one, then press Ctrl+Shift+F (Show references to) to jump to the code that uses it.

examples.title: Follow who calls a function
examples.cmd: Click the function name, then Ctrl+Shift+F or Window > Function Call Trees
examples.explain: References show every place the function is used: where the check is called.

examples.title: See the program as boxes
examples.explain: Draws basic blocks with arrows for true/false jumps: ideal for if/else checks.

examples.title: Add a comment
examples.cmd: Click a line, press ;  (semicolon), type, Enter
examples.explain: Notes stay with the project. Use them to record what each step does.

examples.title: Run without the GUI
examples.explain: The headless mode analyses and scripts binaries in bulk.

mistakes: Trusting the decompiler blindly: compare with the assembly when something looks off.
Not waiting for auto-analysis to finish before reading.
Choosing the wrong architecture when importing: the code looks like garbage.
Not renaming as you go: you will re-read the same function many times.
Skipping dynamic checks: run the binary with gdb or ltrace to confirm what you think it does.
